question.stem:
A software company has resources hosted in AWS and on-premises servers. You have been requested to create a decoupled architecture for applications which make use of both resources.
Which of the following options are valid? (Select TWO.)
options: Use SWF to utilize both on-premises servers and EC2 instances for your decoupled application
Use SQS to utilize both on-premises servers and EC2 instances for your decoupled application
Use RDS to utilize both on-premises servers and EC2 instances for your decoupled application
Use DynamoDB to utilize both on-premises servers and EC2 instances for your decoupled application
Use VPC peering to connect both on-premises servers and EC2 instances for your decoupled application
question.explanation: SQS and SWF are the AWS services built for decoupling, and both are reachable over public HTTPS APIs, so producers/consumers (SQS) or workers/deciders (SWF activity workers) can run on EC2 and on on-premises servers alike. RDS and DynamoDB are databases, not decoupling/messaging services. VPC peering connects two VPCs — it cannot connect an on-premises network (that needs VPN or Direct Connect) and is networking, not decoupling.

concept: Hybrid decoupling: SQS / SWF with workers on EC2 and on-premises
tests: Knowing which AWS services decouple application components and can be used by both EC2 and on-premises servers.
expected: SQS (message queue) and SWF (workflow with activity workers that can run anywhere). Triggers: "decoupled architecture" + "on-premises and AWS" → SQS / SWF — both are public API endpoints reachable from anywhere.
why_not: RDS and DynamoDB are databases, not decoupling services; VPC peering only connects VPCs (not on-prem) and is networking, not decoupling.
